title: How To Teach Your Classroom Management Plan https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2011/08/13/how-to-teach-a-classroom-management-plan/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes teaching the classroom management plan as the single most important task of the first day of school, arguing that expertise in classroom management correlates directly with teacher effectiveness, confidence, and relationship quality. He offers a set of directives for delivering the lesson: be clear about what counts as following or breaking rules, be passionate and dynamic in demonstrating them, and use a 'how-not' contrarian technique where the teacher role-plays rule-breaking behavior so students can recognize it. He also recommends making the lesson interactive through role-play, being thorough enough to eliminate ambiguity, and testing comprehension by having students demonstrate the rules themselves. Practically, he suggests roughly an hour a day of initial teaching during the first week, tapering to daily short reviews for three or four weeks and then occasional, roughly weekly, review. The piece closes by tying a vivid, thorough introduction of the plan to students buying into a shared vision of the classroom.
points: Dedicate an hour a day during the first week to teaching the classroom management plan, then review daily for three to four weeks before tapering to weekly.
Use the 'how-not' strategy: role-play common rule-breaking behaviors yourself so students clearly see what not to do.
Make the lesson interactive by having students role-play scenarios and even take turns playing the teacher.
Test comprehension directly by having students demonstrate correct behaviors, or use a written test depending on grade level.
Present the plan with visible passion and physical dynamism, since teacher energy, not subject matter, is what motivates students to buy in.
quotes: Of all the responsibilities you have on the first day of school, teaching your classroom management plan is número uno in importance.
To put it more plainly, experts in classroom management are better teachers—hands down.
Bring your classroom management plan into high-def focus for your students, making it clear and comprehensible—because ambiguity and confusion are the enemies of effective classroom management.

Sit at a student’s desk and show them how not to get your attention, how not to ask a question, or how not to behave during lessons. They must see and experience what isn’t okay in order to fully understand what is.
One of the most common questions I get is how long should it take to teach your classroom management plan. An hour or so a day for the first week of school should be enough for initial learning.
Every student, deep down, when shown the way, wants to do well. They all want to experience the feeling of being more than what they thought they could be.
